strategy.summary: Wälzhammer Präzision is a small, family-owned machining shop under financial stress. It is our 100% source for pump shaft HN 32 mm (1.4404) under a framework agreement that renews automatically each year. It needs cash and work: it is in bank talks, its credit index has worsened, it has short-time work and its second shift is idle. The MD says he cannot sign anything that lowers margin. Our price has already fallen over three renewals while labour and bar costs rose, so there is little room to cut. Our late payment is its legitimate grievance. The latest quote holds the price but asks for 10-day payment. Best path: hold the price, or win a small cut, by trading faster or reliably on-time payment, binding higher volume and a 24-month term. Accept the owner's open-book offer. Do not squeeze margin or threaten an exit. Evidence on its cost structure is thin: there is no should-cost.
strategy.decision_maker: Owner / managing director, who personally decides prices and liquidity matters, with the bank watching closely. Inside sales is only the administrative contact.

persona.style: Personal and direct. Open about its distress (bank, cash) and offers transparency on its calculation. Defensive about margin. Escalates when we pay late.

settles historically well below its ask
we are a small share of its turnover but a steady customer

needs.detail: Wants faster payment and, at a minimum, payment on time; the latest quote asks for 10-day payment.
Short-time work in machining and the second shift on hold; it can take additional parts at short notice.
Binding volume and a longer term give it comfort with its banks; our forecast is rising.
Cannot accept a margin reduction; cost drivers over 12 months point upward.
Quality has improved, with rolling ppm now better than the peer median, and the relationship has run for a long time.

constraints.detail: The bank monitors it monthly; liquidity is the binding constraint.
Margin floor: the MD will not sign anything that lowers margin, likely because of bank or covenant pressure.
Prices are fixed per calendar year. Changes and termination both need 90 days' notice, so the windows close around early October; otherwise the contract auto-extends.
Holds 100% quota. The only alternative, Dralveck, quoted higher on old data, although we own the tooling.

levers.why: Its strongest need. Faster payment is worth far more to it than to us, so trade it for price or for holding the price.
A rising forecast fills idle machines; commit it as binding volume within our real need.
Take up the owner's own offer to walk through his calculation, to test the cost-increase claims respectfully.
Short-time work shows it wants work; frame volume as help, not pressure.
The alloy surcharge has fallen recently; this counters claims of rising material cost.
Bar has come off its peak; this counters the 12-month bar argument.
Power costs are down; use as a fresh filler fact.
Anchors any discussion at the current price.
Reminds it that past asks settled lower; use gently.
On-time delivery is below the contract target; a late fresh fact, framed as a request for a service commitment.

trades.why: Cash is its top need; give shorter payment in exchange for price, ideally in the last round.
Idle capacity: binding volume within our forecast need is worth more to it than it costs us.
Twenty-four months gives it bank comfort and planning security; 36 adds nothing.
Only if it demands one. The recent trend in its material indices is flat to down, so a clause at a lower base price can suit us; price the clause risk on our side.
It has spare capacity; no need to pay for changes to lead time.
Quality is improving; it may accept a target at no premium, which helps given repeated dimension defects.

price_view.reasoning: Price cut over three renewals while labour and bar costs rose. Weighted drivers support a modest increase. The only rival quote was dearer. Finances are weak and the MD rejects margin cuts. A small concession is possible only in return for cash or volume. There is no should-cost, so the evidence is thin.

do: Acknowledge our late payments and commit to paying on time
Show respect for the owner and the long relationship
Frame volume and term as partnership
dont: Threaten termination or a move to Dralveck
Ask open cost questions without our own data

traps: Citing the exit window, tooling ownership or the second source as a threat would alarm a fragile single source; contract_clause:320011:1f580e9a, tooling:320011:3738937e and sourcing_position:320011:1cc87439 stay in reserve only

strategy.writer_notes: Open by owning our payment lapses and promising reliable on-time payment. Hold the faster-payment concession for the final round where possible. Accept the owner's invitation to review his calculation together. Answer any cost-driver claim with the recent softening of the alloy surcharge and bar indices. Keep a warm, personal tone addressed to the owner.
questions_to_ask: Could we take up your offer to walk through your calculation together before we settle the price?
Which payment arrangement would help your liquidity most, and how would you reflect it in the price?
How much additional volume could you take on with your current crew, and what would a binding commitment be worth to you?
What would help you return to the agreed on-time delivery level?

findings.text: No should-cost exists for part:320011, so how far the price sits above full cost cannot be measured. The only cost view is the category team's driver weights (labour 31%, cold-drawn bar 18%, alloy surcharge 11%, power 5%; about 35% unexplained). The owner offered to walk us through his calculation (hourly rates, material). Taking that up is the only way to build a should-cost.

Weighted 12-month driver change is about +3.5% on the price: labour +0.82%, bar +2.21%, alloy surcharge +0.65%, power -0.19%. Cost drivers therefore support a modest increase of roughly 3-3.5%, not a cut. The bar rise is mostly base effect: the index is 2.3% below its June 2026 peak, and the alloy surcharge fell 5.5% since June. The recent trend is flat to down.

The price has fallen from 34.74 (2023) to 34.07 (2024) to 33.06 (2025), and was held at 33.06 for 2026 (-4.8% overall). Over the same period labour rose about 11% from its low and bar about 12.6% from its low. Its margin has likely been compressed, which fits its weak finances.

The new quote holds the price at 33.06 but asks for 10-day payment instead of 30. At the 3% skonto, that is effectively a 3% price ask (about 32.07 equivalent if the discount is kept). Paying faster is a trade lever, not a concession to give away.

The only competitive benchmark is old: Dralveck quoted 36.00 versus Wälzhammer's 35.00 in Feb 2024. The current price is about 8% below that rival quote, so there is no market evidence that the price is too high.

The bar +12.3% figure is checkable and supports their claim of a cost increase

findings.text: Decision makers: a family-owned firm of 55 staff where the owner/managing director personally handles prices and liquidity. In June the owner offered to walk us through their calculation (hourly rates, material). This is an open-book opening we can use to test cost claims. A sales contact change (inside sales) is only an administrative route.

The supplier is in financial stress:
- It is negotiating with its banks after two weak years.
- Its credit index worsened from 230 to 302.
- Its equity ratio is 20.3%.
- The MD says the bank is watching every month and 'I cannot sign anything that lowers our margin now'.
This is a hard constraint: a price cut that lowers its margin will likely be refused or need bank consent. Liquidity-improving trades are the way to move it.

It needs cash. The MD asked twice for earlier payment. Its 2026-07-20 email complains our invoices are overdue again and threatens to review conditions. Our record backs the complaint: 47.3% of invoices paid late, 32.4% over 10 days late, max 32 days late, and 7 discounts taken after the skonto period. This is its strongest grievance; we must expect it to be raised and should fix it before asking for anything.

It needs volume. Part of machining is on short-time work, citing weak machinery orders. The second shift has been on hold since spring, and sales said they could take additional parts at short notice. Extra parts or volume (8670 planned vs 7040 last 12 months) and a longer commitment are valuable currency.

Its negotiating position is weak:
- Our spend is about 3.6% of its turnover.
- We own the tooling.
- A qualified alternative exists (Dralveck, though it quoted higher in 2024).
- The contract renewal notice is still open until 2026-10-02.
Historically it settles well below its ask (last renewal: asked +3.5%, settled 0%).

Red flags:
- It is a supply risk: delivery on-time fell from 95.8% to 88.9% (target 95%), possibly linked to stress.
- An exit or squeeze could destabilise it.
Quality is improving (425 ppm vs 765), which it will use as recognition.

findings.text: Framework agreement ctr:4600070280 covers only part:320011 (pump shaft HN 32 mm, 1.4404). Prices are fixed per calendar year. A change needs written notice at least 90 days before year end, i.e. by about 2026-10-02 for 2027. The agreement runs to 2026-12-31 and auto-extends 12 months unless either side terminates with 90 days' notice, also due by about 2026-10-02. Both the supplier's increase notice window and our exit window close within days of this data date.

Commercial terms: 30 days net with 3% skonto within 10 days, which is shorter than our 60-day standard. Incoterm is EXW and lead time 28 days. The quality agreement sets a 95% OTD target and EUR 150 per supplier-caused complaint. OTD has slipped to 88.9% against the 95% target (95.8% a year earlier). This is a contractual shortfall we can raise, although peers' median is lower at 84.6%.

History: three renewals with an average ask of +1.4% and an average settlement of -1.6%, a gap of about 3 points. Asked/settled: 2024 +1.5/-1.9, 2025 -0.7/-3.0, 2026 +3.5/0. Price fell from 34.74 to 33.06 (-4.8%). The supplier usually ends well below its ask, but the cumulative cuts on a weakening supplier limit how much further we can go.

Dependency is mixed:
- We hold 100% quota with the supplier, which has been approved since 2015.
- Hollerau owns the tooling, and Dralveck (sup:70210) is qualified at 0% quota.
- Dralveck's only benchmark quote (rfq:6000000109, 2024) was EUR 36.00, about 9% dearer, so switching costs price.
- We are about 3.6% of the supplier's turnover. It is on short-time work and in bank talks, so it needs our volume and cash.

Supplier health is deteriorating: equity ratio 20.3% and credit index 302, up from 230 (higher is worse). The managing director said he cannot sign margin cuts and asked for faster payment. Our late payment (47% of invoices late) is a legitimate grievance for them. Squeezing price risks supply on a single-sourced part. Trading faster payment for price is the natural lever.

findings.text: Delivery has slipped from a peak of 95.8-96% on-time (rolling to 2025-09/2025-12) to 85.7-88.9% since, below the 95% contract target. The peer median is lower (84.6%), so the argument works against the contract target, not against peers. When late, deliveries average 10.7 days late (max 13) in the last 12 months.

Quality on the single part 320011: 9 of 10 notifications were supplier-caused, including repeated dimension and marking defects. Rolling ppm peaked at 1040 (2025Q4) and is now 425, slightly better than the peer median of 457, so the trend argues its case. Recharges are small (EUR 1050 in total; EUR 300 in the last 12 months), and the 8D overdue at 2026Q2 has been cleared.

The volume outlook is up: the 2026-09 forecast is 8670 pcs for the next 12 months against 7040 ordered in the last 12 months (+23%), and it has been shared with the supplier. With part of its machining on short-time work and the second shift on hold, this volume is valuable to it and is our main trade currency, alongside faster payment.

The price is flat at 33.06 since 2025 and down 4.8% from 34.74 in 2023. It already conceded in earlier rounds, which supports its claim to have little room. The last renewal settled at +0.0% against an ask of +3.5%.

Order execution is clean: rush and change lines are few, quantity variance is 0.22%, and confirmed dates match requested dates on recent purchase orders. Note the data issue that requested and confirmed dates differ by 10-30 points (KNOWN_ISSUES 1), so the delivery figures are somewhat thin.

arguments.text: Our price has gone down three renewals in a row (34.74 to 34.07 to 33.06, then held flat for 2026), while our costs rose. We have already given Hollerau about 4.8 % in real money. A further cut is not justified. Holding 33.06 is itself a concession.

Our cost drivers point up. Cold-drawn bar is +12.3 % in 12 months (about 18 % of cost). Labour is +2.7 % (about 31 %). The 1.4404 alloy surcharge is +5.9 % (about 11 %). Weighted, that comes to roughly +3.6 % cost pressure on this shaft, which matches our 3.5 % ask last year, and we settled at 0.

Hollerau pays late: 47.3 % of invoices are late, 32.4 % more than 10 days late, up to 32 days. Discount was taken after the period 7 times. We are financing our customer. Paying on time, or in 10 days, is the fair basis before anyone talks about price.

Our performance has improved. The rolling score is back to class A (92.3). ppm fell from 1040 to 425, and there are no overdue 8Ds. Delivery runs at 88.9 % last 12 months with max 13 days late, versus 21 before.
The only benchmark was in our favour. Dralveck quoted 36 against our 35 in 2024, and a switch would mean qualification effort and risk for a part we have run since 2015.
We are open-book. Our owner offered to walk Hollerau through hourly rates and material. We have nothing to hide.

weak_points: Our finances are visibly weak: bank talks, credit index worsened from 230 to 302, short-time work, equity 20 %. The customer may fear for continuity, or exploit it.
We have idle capacity (second shift on hold) and need the work. This undercuts any scarcity argument.
Electricity is -3.7 % in 12 months and -43 % versus 2022. Alloy surcharge is -13 % from its 36-month peak, and bar is below its 2022 high.
Quality had a bad stretch in 2025 (7 complaints, 1040 ppm), and delivery is still below the 95 % OTD target in the contract. One 8D was overdue in Q2.
Hollerau owns the tooling, so moving to Dralveck is technically easy.
The cost weights are the customer's own estimate and we have no should-cost. Our real margin is unknown to them, and opening the books could reveal fat or distress.
Our 2024 quote was 35 while the contract price was 34.07, which is inconsistent.
Our MD signalled publicly that we cannot accept margin cuts and the bank watches us. That shows dependence.
wants: Payment in 10 days (or at minimum strict 30 days net, with skonto only within the period). For 10-day payment we could accept skonto-equivalent value, i.e. hold price or give about 1 %.
Binding annual volume at the new forecast level (around 8,500 pcs), ideally with a take-or-pay element.
A 24-month term to show our bank.
Additional parts to fill the second shift. Bundling would justify a small price reduction.
Optionally an index clause on bar or alloy surcharge rather than a fixed-price cut.
red_lines: No price below 33.06 without faster payment plus binding volume. Any cut must be margin-neutral, funded by cash or volume.
No longer payment terms than 30 days.
No higher chargebacks or tougher ppm penalties without a price adjustment.
No fixed price for longer than 12 months without an index clause or volume commitment.
Not signing anything the bank would read as lower margin.
red_team.opening: Thank Hollerau for the long partnership and point to the improved scorecard. State that we are holding 33.06 for 2027 despite bar +12.3 % and labour +2.7 %, after three years of reductions. In return we ask for payment within 10 days, as in quote:7300056, and that past overdue invoices be settled. Offer the owner's open-book walkthrough, and signal willingness to discuss a small concession if Hollerau commits to about 8,500 pcs per year over 24 months and considers extra machined parts for our free capacity.

rebuttals.answer: You are right that the price has come down over the past renewals and held flat this year, and we value that. Those settlements were agreed together, in years when your forecast volumes and our order book grew, so they reflect a working partnership rather than a gift. Our starting point is the price we pay today. We are not asking you to cut your margin; we want to find terms that work for both of us.

We accept that labour and bar have risen over the year, and we take that seriously. The picture is mixed, though. The alloy surcharge and cold-drawn bar have both eased in recent months, and power costs are lower than a year ago. The weights are only estimates, so the honest way to settle this is the walk-through of your calculation your owner offered, rather than a headline sum of the rising drivers alone.

This point is fair, and we do not dispute it. Our payment discipline has not been good enough, and we apologise. We commit to paying on time from now on. We are also ready to talk about faster payment as part of the overall package, because we understand how much reliable cash matters to you right now.

Thank you for that work. On-time delivery has slipped from a year ago, however, and is still below the target in our quality agreement. We would welcome a joint plan to get back to target, and we would value a ppm commitment that locks in the gains you have made.

That benchmark was a routine check, and we value the long relationship on this part. A single quote from some time ago says little about today's price, so it is not a basis for adjusting prices now. We would rather build the case on current facts: volume, payment and your actual costs.

We appreciate this openness and would gladly take up the offer. Walking through your hourly rates and material together is the fairest way to agree a price that keeps your business healthy and stays competitive for us.

press: Our forecast for the coming year is clearly above what we ordered over the past year, and we would be glad to discuss committing part of it as binding volume to help fill your machines.
A longer agreement with reliable, faster payment from our side could give you planning security and support with your bank, and we would like to reflect that together in the price.
We noticed that power costs and the alloy surcharge have softened recently, and we would like to look at that together when we go through your calculation.
Could we agree a short plan to bring on-time delivery back to the level set in our quality agreement?
We would welcome a ppm commitment that secures the quality improvement you have achieved.
